intro: How tall is a seventh grader? Is this coin fair? Does more sleep really go with better grades? None of these questions has a single answer you can look up. Each one asks about a whole group, or about chance, and the honest answer comes from collecting data and reading it carefully. That is what statistics and probability do. They turn a pile of numbers into a picture, a few summary values and a claim you can defend.

In this unit you will measure a class and describe it with dot plots, histograms and box plots, with the mean and median for the center and the range, IQR and MAD for the spread. You will put a number on chance, from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain, list every outcome of a compound event, run simulations, and learn why a random sample of 50 students can tell you something true about 800. Finally you will plot two measurements at once, fit a line by eye, read its slope and intercept, and sort categories into two-way tables.

Along the way you will learn what data can and cannot prove. A bigger sample beats a smaller one, but a biased sample of a million is worse than a random sample of a hundred. Two things that rise together are associated, but association is not cause. By the end you will be able to answer a statistical question from start to finish and explain, with numbers, why your answer deserves to be believed.
bigQuestion: How do we use data and chance to make claims about a whole group that we can actually defend?

timeline.t: Pascal and Fermat exchange letters about games of chance, starting the mathematics of probability
John Graunt studies London's death records and publishes some of the first statistical tables
Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi is published, proving that long runs of trials settle near the true probability
Thomas Bayes's essay on updating probabilities with evidence is published after his death
William Playfair prints some of the first bar charts and line graphs of economic data
The first United States Census counts about 3.9 million people
Legendre and Gauss publish the method of least squares for fitting a line to scattered data
Florence Nightingale uses diagrams of hospital deaths to argue for better sanitation
Francis Galton describes regression and correlation from measurements of parents and children
Karl Pearson introduces the chi-square test for comparing counts in tables
John Tukey's Exploratory Data Analysis popularizes the box plot

words.d: a question whose answers vary across a group, so it takes data to answer
the sum of the values divided by how many there are
the middle value of the ordered data
Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle half of the data
the average distance of the values from the mean
a picture of the minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum
a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely an event is
the organized list of every possible outcome
a sample where every member of the population had an equal chance of being picked
a graph with one point for each pair of measurements
a straight line drawn through the middle of a linear cloud of points
a table that counts how many fall into each pair of categories

test.q: What is the mean of 4, 8, 9 and 15?

test.why: In order: 2, 5, 6, 9, 11. The middle value is 6. The mean is 6.6.
Lower half 3, 5, 7, 9 gives Q1 = 6; upper half 11, 13, 15, 17 gives Q3 = 14. IQR = 14 − 6 = 8.

test.q: Data: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 80. Which measure of center best describes a typical value?
choices: the mean, because it uses every value
the maximum, because it is the largest
the median, because 80 is an outlier that pulls the mean up
test.why: The mean is 152 ÷ 6, about 25.3, above five of the six values. The median is 15.

test.q: A bag has 2 red and 6 blue marbles. What is P(red)?
A spinner is spun 25 times and lands on green 10 times. What is the experimental probability of green?
You flip two coins and roll one die. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
Two dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show an even number?
test.why: Each die shows even with probability 1/2, and the rolls are independent: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

test.q: Which is a random sample of a school's students?
choices: 30 students chosen by a random number generator from the full enrollment list
30 students in the library after school
the 30 students on the honor roll
30 students who reply to a text survey
test.why: Only the random draw from the full list gives every student an equal chance.

test.q: In a random sample of 75 students, 30 prefer soccer. The school has 1,500 students. About how many prefer soccer?
What is the slope of a line through (3, 8) and (7, 20)?
Using y = 4x − 6, what is y when x = 5?
18 of 60 girls and 12 of 30 boys ride the bus. Which group has the higher share of bus riders?
choices: it cannot be told from counts
test.why: 18 ÷ 60 = 0.3 and 12 ÷ 30 = 0.4. Compare percents, not counts, when groups differ in size.

test.q: A scatter plot of hours of sleep and quiz score rises to the right. Which describes it?
test.why: As sleep increases, scores tend to increase, so the association is positive.

write.prompt: Two classes took the same quiz. Class A: mean 78, MAD 4. Class B: mean 84, MAD 4. Is Class B really doing better, or could the difference be chance? Find how many MADs apart the means are, decide, and explain each step. Then say what else you would want to know before trusting the conclusion.
tips: State your decision in the first sentence.
Show the subtraction and the division that give the number of MADs.
Explain what a difference of that many MADs means about how much the two groups overlap.
Say how the classes were chosen and whether that could bias the comparison.
Check your arithmetic a second time before you finish.
